text: {{c1::Germ}} cells (spermatogonia) maintain the germ pool and produce primary spermatocytes
extra: Photo credit: OpenStax, CC BY 4.0

text: The first stage of spermatogenesis is {{c1::DNA replication (interphase)}} of {{c2::spermatogonia}} to generate the {{c2::primary spermatocytes}}
extra: Photo credit: OpenStax, CC BY 4.0

text: After the primary spermatocyte has been formed, it undergoes {{c1::meiosis I}} to become a(n) {{c2::secondary spermatocyte}}
extra: At this stage, the spermatocyte goes from diploid to haploid Photo credit: OpenStax, CC BY 4.0

text: After the secondary spermatocyte has been formed, it undergoes {{c1::meiosis II}} to become a(n) {{c2::spermatid}}
extra: Photo credit: OpenStax, CC BY 4.0

text: After spermatids have been formed from secondary spermatocytes, they undergo {{c1::spermiogenesis}} to form {{c2::spermatozoa}}
extra: Photo credit: OpenStax, CC BY 4.0

text: What changes occur during the process of spermiogenesis? - Loss of {{c1::cytoplasmic contents}} - Gain of a(n) {{c1::acrosomal}} cap - Development of a(n) {{c1::flagellum}}
extra: Photo credit: OpenStax, CC BY 4.0

text: After which stage of spermatogenesis does the diploid sperm become haploid? {{c1::Meiosis I (primary spermatocyte to secondary spermatocyte)}}
extra: Photo credit: OpenStax, CC BY 4.0

text: The primary location for the maturation and storage of sperm is the {{c1::epididymis}}
extra: Photo credit: OpenStax, CC BY 4.0

text: In the developing ovaries, primordial germ cells produce {{c1::oogonia}} by {{c2::mitotic}} divisions until gestational weeks {{c3::20}} to {{c3::24}}
extra: Photo credit: OpenStax, CC BY 4.0

text: {{c1::DNA replication (interphase)::Process}} of oogonia generates the {{c2::primary oocytes}} (arrested in prophase 1)
extra: This process ends shortly before birth Photo credit: OpenStax, CC BY 4.0

text: Beginning at ovulation, primary oocytes (diploid) begin to complete {{c1::meiosis I}} to form {{c2::secondary oocytes}} (haploid)
extra: Photo credit: OpenStax, CC BY 4.0

text: After fertilization, the secondary oocyte completes {{c1::meiosis II}} to form a(n) {{c2::ovum}}
extra: Photo credit: OpenStax, CC BY 4.0

text: Primary oocytes are arrested in prophase I of meiosis I for years until {{c1::ovulation}}
extra: Photo credit: OpenStax, CC BY 4.0

text: Secondary oocytes are arrested in metaphase II of meiosis II until {{c1::fertilization}}
extra: Photo credit: OpenStax, CC BY 4.0

text: During which week of gestation does gastrulation occur? {{c1::Week 3}}
extra: gasTRIlation Photo credit: OpenStax College, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

text: What is the embryonic origin of the spinal cord? {{c1::Neural tube (neuroectoderm)}}

text: What is the embryonic origin of the alveolar, tracheal, and bronchial epithelium? {{c1::Endoderm}}
extra: However airway cartilage is from mesoderm

text: What is the embryonic origin of the adrenal medulla? {{c1::Neural crest}}
extra: In contrast, the adrenal cortex is derived from mesoderm

text: Supplemental maternal {{c2::folic acid (vitamin B9)}} in early pregnancy decreases risk of {{c1::neural tube}} defects
extra: Take this at least 1 month prior to conception and during early pregnancy (give B9 for 9 months of pregnancy)

text: What is the embryonic origin of PNS neurons? {{c1::Neural crest}}

text: Neurulation begins in the {{c1::third}} week of fetal development
extra: Photo credit: OpenStax College, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

text: The {{c2::notochord}} induces the overlying ectoderm to form the {{c1::neural plate (neuroectoderm)}}
extra: Photo credit: OpenStax College, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

text: By the end of the third week, neural {{c2::folds}} grow over the midline and fuse to form the {{c1::neural tube}}
extra: Photo credit: OpenStax College, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

text: During closure of neural folds, the {{c1::neural crest}} cells form from neuroectoderm
extra: Neural crest cells migrate to distant sites by the end of week 5 Photo credit: OpenStax College, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

text: What is the embryonic origin of CNS neurons? {{c1::Neural tube (neuroectoderm)}}

text: The embryonic {{c1::notochord}} becomes the {{c2::nucleus pulposus}} of the intervertebral discs in adults
What is the embryonic origin of melanocytes? {{c1::Neural crest}}
Within which week of embryogenesis does the neural tube close? {{c1::Week 4}}
What is the embryonic origin of the odontoblasts and bones of the skull? {{c1::Neural crest}}
What is the embryonic origin of the muscle, bone, and connective tissue? {{c1::Meso::Endo/Meso/Ecto}}derm
What is the embryonic origin of the blood and lymphatics? {{c1::Meso::Endo/Meso/Ecto}}derm
What is the embryonic origin of the kidneys? {{c1::Meso::Endo/Meso/Ecto}}derm
What is the embryonic origin of the ovaries/testis? {{c1::Meso::Endo/Meso/Ecto}}derm
What pathology is associated with disruption of the cranial end of the neural tube? {{c1::Anencephaly}}
extra: Photo credit: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, National Center on Birth Defects and Developmental Disabilities, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

text: What pathology is associated with disruption of the caudal end of the neural tube? {{c1::Spina bifida}}
extra: Photo credit: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

text: What is the embryonic origin of the gut tube epithelium and most major organs (e.g., lungs, liver, gallbladder, pancreas)? {{c1::Endo::Endo/Meso/Ecto}}derm
Blood flows down a {{c1::decreasing}} pressure gradient: artery → arteriole → capillary → venule → vein.
extra: High pressure + thick wall → low pressure + thin wall.

text: From inside out, the three vessel tunics are the {{c1::intima}} (endothelium), {{c2::media}} (smooth muscle/elastin), and {{c3::adventitia}} (connective tissue).
extra: Same plan in every vessel; local pressure sculpts each layer's thickness.

text: The wavy elastin sheet separating the arterial intima from the media is the {{c1::internal elastic lamina}}.
extra: External elastic lamina bounds media from adventitia.

text: Vasa vasorum (vessels of the vessel wall) are more numerous in {{c1::veins}}.
extra: Venous luminal blood is O2-poor, low-pressure → wall fed worse from the lumen.

text: All vessels are lined by a {{c1::simple squamous}} epithelium sealed by tight junctions: the endothelium.
extra: Aligned to flow.

text: Endothelial {{c1::nitric oxide}} relaxes medial smooth muscle → {{c2::vasodilation}}.
Endothelium secretes {{c1::von Willebrand factor}} → platelet adhesion at vessel injury.
Atherosclerotic plaque begins at the {{c1::injured endothelium}} (hypertension, smoking, cholesterol).
extra: Intima; the thinnest cell of the wall.

text: Which artery type (aorta, carotid) has a media of {{c1::fenestrated elastic laminae}} and buffers the pulse via the {{c2::Windkessel}} effect? {{c3::Elastic artery}}
extra: Stretch in systole, recoil in diastole → pulsatile flow becomes continuous.

text: Which artery type (radial, tibial, splenic) has a media dominated by {{c1::smooth muscle}} and regulates {{c2::caliber}} to distribute blood? {{c3::Muscular artery}}
extra: The media component names the artery.

text: The stain that reveals elastin, separating elastic from muscular artery, is {{c1::Weigert}}.
extra: Elastic laminae as stacked dark lines.

text: Which vessel (< 0.5 mm) sets peripheral {{c1::resistance}}, the main control of arterial pressure? {{c2::Arteriole}}
extra: Wall nearly as thick as the lumen is wide.

text: At the capillary bed entry, the {{c1::precapillary sphincter}} gates flow in waves by local demand.
extra: Short sparse-muscle vessel at the transition = metarteriole.

text: A {{c1::portal}} system passes blood through {{c2::two}} capillary beds in series (hepatic portal vein; renal glomerulus).
The capillary wall is reduced to just {{c1::endothelium + basal lamina}}: no media, no adventitia.
extra: Pericytes outside give support and repair.

text: Which capillary has no pores and a continuous basal lamina (muscle, nerve, connective tissue)? {{c1::Continuous}}
extra: The sealed pattern.

text: Which capillary has endothelial {{c1::pores (fenestrations)}} but a {{c2::continuous}} basal lamina (kidney, gut, endocrine glands)? {{c3::Fenestrated}}
extra: Fast filtration/absorption without losing cells.

text: Which capillary has fenestrated endothelium AND a {{c1::discontinuous}} basal lamina, letting whole {{c2::cells}} pass (liver, hemopoietic organs)? {{c3::Sinusoid}}
Fenestrated vs sinusoid capillary: the discriminator is the {{c1::basal lamina}} (continuous vs discontinuous).
extra: Both have fenestrated endothelium; the endothelium alone confuses them.

text: Which vessel has three tunics under low pressure: no elastic laminae, scant media, thick adventitia, wide lumen? {{c1::Vein}}
extra: Opposite of the same-caliber artery (thick wall, small round lumen).

text: Venous valves are semilunar folds of the {{c1::tunica intima}}; the {{c2::skeletal muscle pump}} drives venous return.
extra: Incompetent valve → reflux → varices.

text: The lymphatic capillary is blind-ended and highly permeable because it {{c1::lacks tight junctions}} (overlapping flaps + anchoring filaments).
extra: Admits fluid, large proteins, and cells that the sealed blood capillary excludes.

text: Lymphatic vessels resemble veins but have many more {{c1::valves}}.
extra: No heart to push lymph; each squeeze becomes a step forward.

text: The lymphatic system is absent in the {{c1::CNS}}, {{c2::bone marrow}}, {{c3::cartilage}}, {{c4::bone}}, and {{c5::epithelia}} (epidermis, cornea).
extra: Avascular-for-lymph tissues; excess fluid drains otherwise.

text: Neurons and most glia derive from the {{c1::neuroectoderm}} (neural tube wall).
extra: Origin predicts function.

text: In the PNS (ganglion neurons + Schwann cells), the origin is the {{c1::neural crest}}.
extra: Neural crest also gives melanocytes and adrenal medulla.

text: Which glial cell is the exception, arising from {{c1::mesoderm}} (monocyte lineage)? {{c2::Microglia}}
extra: Hence the resident macrophage of the CNS.

text: Which neuron type has a single axon and multiple dendrites and is the most common (motor, interneuron, Purkinje)? {{c1::Multipolar}}
Which neuron type has one dendrite and one axon at opposite poles? {{c1::Bipolar}}
Bipolar neurons are restricted to the {{c1::retina}}, {{c2::olfactory mucosa}}, and {{c3::cochlear/vestibular ganglia}}.
Which neuron type has one trunk that branches in a {{c1::T}} and is the sensory neuron of the dorsal root ganglion? {{c2::Pseudounipolar}}
extra: Born bipolar; the two processes fuse. True unipolar does not exist in humans.

text: By function, a neuron carrying signals between others (internal bridge, the majority) is an {{c1::interneuron}}.
extra: Afferent = brings in; efferent = sends to effector.

text: The neuron cell body (perikaryon) is the {{c1::trophic}} center; its nucleus is large, spherical, and pale, i.e. {{c2::euchromatic}}, with a prominent nucleolus.
extra: A cell in very high protein synthesis.

text: Which basophilic bodies are rough ER + polyribosomes, staining dark for their {{c1::RNA}}? {{c2::Nissl bodies}}
Nissl bodies are present in the perikaryon and {{c1::dendrites}}, but absent from the {{c2::axon hillock and axon}}.
extra: The practical way to tell a dendrite from an axon on a slide.

text: Which brown pigment accumulates in the aged neuron (lysosomal digestion residue), a sign of age not disease? {{c1::Lipofuscin}}
The neuron's input pole, which tapers, branches, and bears {{c1::spines}} (substrate of plasticity), is the {{c2::dendrite}}.
extra: Contains Nissl.

text: The axon leaves at the {{c1::axon hillock}}, the {{c2::trigger}} zone where the action potential is born.
extra: Uniform caliber, no Nissl.

text: Because the axon makes no protein, it depends on active {{c1::axonal transport}}, running on {{c2::microtubules}} using ATP.
extra: Diffusion alone → years across a 1 m axon.

text: Anterograde axonal transport (body → terminal) uses {{c1::kinesin}}; retrograde (terminal → body) uses {{c2::dynein}}.
Rabies virus and tetanus toxin reach the CNS by the {{c1::retrograde}} route, hijacking {{c2::dynein}}.
extra: Neurotropic via axonal transport, not via blood.

text: At the chemical synapse, the action potential opens {{c1::calcium}} channels in the bouton, and Ca2+ triggers {{c2::vesicle fusion}}.
extra: Neurotransmitter into the cleft → postsynaptic receptors.

text: Which rarer synapse joins cells by {{c1::gap junctions}}, passing ions directly in a {{c2::bidirectional}}, near-instant signal? {{c3::Electrical synapse}}
Which glial cell buffers extracellular {{c1::potassium}}, recycles neurotransmitter, and feeds the neuron {{c2::glucose}}? {{c3::Astrocyte}}
The blood-brain barrier is made by endothelial {{c1::tight junctions}}, induced by the {{c2::astrocyte}} perivascular foot.
extra: Oligodendrocyte myelinates; microglia phagocytoses; only the astrocyte touches the vessel.

text: The {{c1::protoplasmic}} astrocyte (short processes) lives in gray matter; the {{c2::fibrous}} astrocyte (long processes) lives in white matter.
extra: Astrocyte scar after injury = gliosis.

text: CNS myelin is built by the {{c1::oligodendrocyte}} (myelinates several axons at once); PNS myelin by the {{c2::Schwann cell}} (one internode of one axon).
extra: Oligodendrocyte serves many; Schwann serves one.

text: The myelin-free gap rich in {{c1::sodium}} channels where the action potential regenerates, allowing {{c2::saltatory}} conduction, is the {{c3::node of Ranvier}}.
extra: Myelin insulates and forces the signal to jump node to node.

text: A PNS unmyelinated axon is still wrapped by a Schwann cell but {{c1::without a spiral wrap}} (several axons in the cell's grooves).
extra: Schwann around it is not the same as myelin.

text: Which cell is the resident macrophage of the CNS, phagocytosing debris and triggering inflammation on injury? {{c1::Microglia}}
Cells lining the ventricles and central canal are {{c1::ependymal}} cells; over capillaries they specialize into the {{c2::choroid plexus}}, which makes CSF.
Which PNS glial cell wraps the neuron cell bodies inside ganglia, insulating them? {{c1::Satellite cells}}
extra: Unrelated to the muscle satellite cell (a stem cell).

text: Gray matter holds {{c1::cell bodies}}, {{c2::dendrites}}, and {{c3::synapses}} (neuropil); white matter is {{c4::myelinated axons}}, whose myelin gives the color.
In the cerebral cortex the gray matter lies on the {{c1::outside}}, in {{c2::six}} layers (the basis of Brodmann's map).
The cerebellar cortex has three layers: molecular, {{c1::Purkinje}} (single row of giant cells, the only output), and granular.
In the spinal cord the gray matter lies {{c1::inside}}, in an {{c2::H (butterfly)}} shape.
extra: Cortex gray outside, cord gray inside; no single rule.

text: The three peripheral nerve sheaths are the {{c1::endoneurium}} (each fiber), {{c2::perineurium}} (each fascicle), and {{c3::epineurium}} (whole nerve, with vessels).
extra: Perineurium is also a barrier: its cells have tight junctions.

text: The sensory (dorsal root) ganglion has pseudounipolar neurons and {{c1::makes no synapse}}; the autonomic ganglion has multipolar neurons and is a {{c2::synaptic relay}}.
The meninges, outside in, are {{c1::dura mater}}, {{c2::arachnoid}}, and {{c3::pia mater}}; CSF circulates in the {{c4::subarachnoid}} space.
extra: CSF is made in the choroid plexus and cushions the CNS.

text: The {{c1::primary}} lymphoid organs (bone marrow, thymus) make and educate lymphocytes; the {{c2::secondary}} ones (lymph node, spleen, MALT) are where the response happens.
Any molecule recognized as foreign and able to trigger the immune response is an {{c1::antigen}}.
extra: Core job: tell self from non-self.

text: The activated B lymphocyte does not secrete antibody directly: it becomes a {{c1::plasma cell}}, which secretes the antibody.
extra: Resting B carries surface IgM/IgD as its antigen antenna.

text: The surface marker of the T lymphocyte (cell-mediated response, cell-to-cell contact) is the {{c1::TCR}}.
Which T cell kills infected/tumor cells with {{c1::perforin}}? {{c2::Cytotoxic (CD8) T cell}}
Which T cell coordinates the response by secreting {{c1::interleukins}}? {{c2::Helper (CD4) T cell}}
Which T cell suppresses the response and prevents autoimmunity? {{c1::Regulatory T cell (Treg)}}
Which lymphocyte belongs to {{c1::innate}} immunity, killing abnormal cells with no prior sensitization, no TCR, and no memory? {{c2::NK cell}}
The macrophage not only phagocytoses: it breaks down the antigen and {{c1::presents}} it on its surface for the T cell.
extra: Bridge from engulfing to the specific response.

text: In lymphoid tissue, the fixed {{c1::reticular cell}} produces the {{c2::reticular fiber}} (type III collagen) that forms the scaffold.
extra: Cell makes it; fiber is the product. Fixed macrophage = histiocyte.

text: Rule in every lymphoid organ: the {{c1::fixed}} cells build the structure and filter; the {{c2::free}} cells (lymphocytes, plasma cells) run the response.
The lymphatic {{c1::nodule}} is a temporary, capsule-less structure needing antigenic stimulus; its {{c2::germinal center}} is a site of B-cell proliferation.
extra: Germinal center = tissue reacting. No T cells made there.

text: Gut, respiratory, and urogenital mucosal lymphoid tissue is called {{c1::MALT}}; in the gut it forms {{c2::Peyer's patches}}.
The {{c1::B}} lymphocyte matures in the bone marrow; the {{c2::T}} lymphocyte is educated in the thymus.
In the thymus the {{c1::cortex}} is outer, dark, dense with immature thymocytes; the {{c2::medulla}} is inner and paler.
extra: Lobules are incomplete, so neighboring medullae communicate.

text: The thymic scaffold is made of {{c1::epithelial reticular cells}} (epithelial origin, joined by desmosomes), not ordinary reticular cells.
extra: Scaffold of cells, not collagen fibers. They secrete thymosins.

text: The blood-thymus barrier, isolating immature thymocytes from blood antigens, exists only in the thymic {{c1::cortex}}.
extra: Medulla is not isolated; mature T waits there to enter circulation.

text: Which acidophilic whorl of degenerated epithelial reticular cells is the histologic signature of the thymic medulla? {{c1::Hassall's corpuscle}}
extra: No B cells, no germinal center. See Hassall = thymus.

text: The thymus does not grow with age; it {{c1::involutes}}, peaking near puberty then replaced by fat.
Which lymphoid organ filters {{c1::lymph}} (not blood) via many afferent vessels in and one efferent vessel out at the hilum? {{c2::Lymph node}}
extra: Many in, one out; concentrates filtered lymph.

text: In the lymph node cortex sit the {{c1::B}}-cell nodules; in the paracortex (thymus-dependent area) sit the {{c2::T}} cells.
extra: Medullary cords are rich in plasma cells.

text: Lymphocytes enter the node from the {{c1::blood}}, crossing the paracortical {{c2::high endothelial venules}}, not via the afferent lymph.
Which clear space just under the capsule is the histologic signature of the lymph node, absent in the spleen? {{c1::Subcapsular sinus}}
Which lymphoid organ filters {{c1::blood}} and therefore has no afferent {{c2::lymphatic}} vessels? {{c3::Spleen}}
extra: Blood enters via splenic artery → central artery.

text: The splenic white pulp around the central artery is the {{c1::PALS}} (T-cell sheath) plus the B-cell {{c2::nodules}}.
extra: Same pattern as the node: T around the vessel, B in nodules.

text: The splenic red pulp is the blood compartment: {{c1::cords of Billroth}} (macrophage mesh) and {{c2::sinusoid}} capillaries, where old RBCs are culled.
In the spleen's {{c1::open}} circulation, blood is dumped into the cord and must squeeze back into the sinusoid; a stiff old RBC is trapped and {{c2::phagocytosed}}.
extra: The structure IS the RBC quality-control mechanism.

text: Which signature has an artery running inside the lymphoid tissue, unique to the spleen? {{c1::Nodule with a central artery}}
extra: Reading triad: Hassall = thymus; subcapsular sinus = node; central artery = spleen.

text: After splenectomy, the patient is dangerously vulnerable to {{c1::encapsulated bacteria}}, risking fulminant sepsis.
extra: No splenic filter or red-pulp macrophages to catch them.

text: The {{c1::right}} heart pumps to the pulmonary (lesser) circulation; the {{c2::left}} heart to the systemic (greater) circulation.
extra: Left works at far higher pressure → thicker wall.

text: A vessel is named by flow direction, not oxygen: the pulmonary {{c1::artery}} carries deoxygenated blood, the pulmonary {{c2::veins}} carry oxygenated blood.
extra: Artery leaves the heart; vein returns to it.

text: The heart sits in the {{c1::middle}} mediastinum, wrapped by the pericardial sac.
extra: Sternal angle splits mediastinum into superior and inferior.

text: The heart is off-center: about {{c1::one third}} lies right of the midline and {{c2::two thirds}} to the left.
The heart's {{c1::base}} (superior/posterior) is formed by the atria and gives off the great vessels; the {{c2::apex}} (inferior/left) is the tip of the left ventricle.
The sternocostal (anterior) surface of the heart is mostly the {{c1::right ventricle}}; the right border is the {{c2::right atrium}}.
The coronary (atrioventricular) sulcus separates {{c1::atria from ventricles}}; the interventricular sulci mark the septum. Both carry the {{c2::coronary arteries}}.
The pericardium has an outer {{c1::fibrous}} layer (inelastic) and a {{c2::serous}} layer folded into parietal and visceral sheets; the visceral sheet on the heart is the {{c3::epicardium}}.
extra: Pericardial cavity with lubricating fluid lies between the serous sheets.

text: Because the fibrous pericardium cannot stretch, rapid fluid buildup compresses the heart: {{c1::cardiac tamponade}}.
The upper receiving chambers are the {{c1::atria}}; the lower pumping chambers are the {{c2::ventricles}}.
The left ventricular wall is far thicker because it pumps against the {{c1::systemic}} circulation (high pressure).
extra: Wall thickness records the pressure load.

text: The three cardiac wall layers, inside out, are {{c1::endocardium}}, {{c2::myocardium}} (~95% of thickness), and {{c3::epicardium}}.
Inside the ventricle, the trabeculae carneae and papillary muscles are {{c1::myocardium}}, but the chordae tendineae are {{c2::connective tissue}}.
extra: Explains how the valve cannot evert.

text: The right atrioventricular valve (RA→RV) is the {{c1::tricuspid}} valve, with {{c2::three}} cusps.
The left atrioventricular valve (LA→LV) is the {{c1::mitral (bicuspid)}} valve, with {{c2::two}} cusps.
In systole the papillary muscles pull the {{c1::chordae tendineae}}, holding the AV cusps so they do not collapse into the atrium.
extra: Ruptured chord → cusp everts → regurgitation murmur.

text: Which valves lack chordae tendineae and papillary muscles? {{c1::Semilunar (aortic and pulmonary)}}
extra: Seal passively by cusp shape; only AV valves have that apparatus.

text: The coronary ostia open behind the cusps of the {{c1::aortic}} valve, so the heart is perfused mainly in {{c2::diastole}}.
extra: The heart feeds when it rests, not when it contracts.

text: The fibrous skeleton anchors the valves, prevents orifice dilation, and electrically {{c1::insulates}} the atria from the ventricles.
extra: Dense connective tissue; forces the impulse through the AV node alone.

text: The first heart sound is the closing of the {{c1::atrioventricular}} valves; the second, the closing of the {{c2::semilunar}} valves.
Venous blood of the heart is collected by the {{c1::coronary sinus}}, which empties directly into the {{c2::right atrium}}.
extra: Large collector in the posterior coronary sulcus.

text: From the aortic arch, on the right the {{c1::brachiocephalic trunk}} arises (splitting into right common carotid + right subclavian); on the left, the common carotid and subclavian arise {{c2::directly}}.
extra: The brachiocephalic trunk exists only on the right.

text: The superior and inferior venae cavae return systemic blood to the {{c1::right atrium}}; the four pulmonary veins bring oxygenated blood to the {{c2::left atrium}}.
Direct arteriole-to-venule links that skip the capillary, the {{c1::arteriovenous anastomoses}}, serve mainly {{c2::temperature}} regulation.
extra: Abundant in skin of extremities and mucosae.

text: Most of the blood volume (~{{c1::64%}}) sits at any moment in the {{c2::venous}} system.
extra: The vein is both return path and reservoir.

text: The largest lymphatic vessel, the {{c1::thoracic duct}}, arises from the cisterna chyli and drains all but the {{c2::right upper quadrant}}.
The right upper quadrant is drained by the {{c1::right lymphatic duct}}; both ducts return lymph to the blood at the junction of the {{c2::subclavian}} and {{c3::internal jugular}} veins.
Intestinal lymphatics ({{c1::lacteals}}) carry lipids and fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K), giving lymph a milky look called {{c2::chyle}}.
The three jobs of the lymphatic system are to {{c1::drain}} excess interstitial fluid, {{c2::transport}} dietary fat (chyle), and provide immune {{c3::defense}}.
extra: Both the sewer and the surveillance of the body.

text: Failed lymph drainage (node removed, vessel blocked) pools fluid and swells the limb: {{c1::lymphedema}}.
The lymphatic capillary takes up fluid because its endothelial cells {{c1::overlap like tiles}} (mini-valves) and its basal membrane is {{c2::absent}}; it starts blind-ended.
When the interstitium swells, the {{c1::anchoring filaments}} pull the lymphatic capillary wall open; once inside, pressure shuts the tiles, a one-way door.
extra: The swelling itself opens the drain; wall geometry blocks reflux.

text: Superficial lymphatic networks drain the {{c1::skin}}; deep networks follow the vessels and drain {{c2::muscle and viscera}} — both converge on the same trunks.
The node throttles flow with many {{c1::afferent}} vessels in but a single {{c2::efferent}} out at the hilum; the slowdown lets macrophages filter.
extra: The pinched shape is the filter, by design.

text: The main superficial node chains sit in the neck, epitrochlear (elbow), {{c1::axilla}}, near the clavicle, the {{c2::inguinal}} region, and popliteal.
extra: Hand infection → epitrochlear + axillary; foot lesion → inguinal.

text: The breast drains mainly to the {{c1::axillary}} nodes, the route breast cancer tends to spread along first.
extra: Axillary assessment is part of staging.

text: Waldeyer's ring, guarding the pharyngeal inlet, is formed by the {{c1::pharyngeal}}, {{c2::palatine}}, {{c3::tubal}}, and {{c4::lingual}} tonsils.
The aggregated lymphoid nodules of the ileum and appendix that monitor gut contents are the {{c1::Peyer's patches}}.
extra: Part of MALT.

text: The trunk draining the abdominal viscera (stomach, intestines, pancreas, spleen, liver) is the {{c1::intestinal}} trunk; the one draining lower limbs, abdominal wall, and pelvis is the {{c2::lumbar}} trunk.
extra: Bronchomediastinal → thorax/lungs/heart; jugular → head/neck; subclavian → upper limbs.

text: The sac-like dilation at the base of the thoracic duct is the {{c1::cisterna chyli}}, receiving the {{c2::lumbar and intestinal}} trunks.
extra: Ascends in front of the spine from L2.

text: The smaller {{c1::right lymphatic duct}} drains only the {{c2::right upper quadrant}} (right head/neck, right upper limb, right hemithorax).
Each lymphatic duct returns lymph to the blood at the {{c1::venous angle}}, the junction of the {{c2::subclavian}} and {{c3::internal jugular}} veins.
extra: Thoracic duct on the left, right duct on the right.

text: Injury to the thoracic duct (e.g., thoracic surgery) leaks milky chyle into the pleura: {{c1::chylothorax}}.
extra: Milky because it carries dietary fat.

text: With no heart to pump it, lymph rises by three forces: contraction of the wall {{c1::smooth muscle}}, the skeletal {{c2::muscle}} pump, and the {{c3::respiratory}} pump.
extra: Valves, even more numerous than in veins, turn each squeeze into a step upward.

text: The heart's two pumps feed two circuits in {{c1::series}}, not in parallel: all blood leaving one passes through the other before completing the loop.
Venous blood reaches the right atrium through three doors: the {{c1::superior vena cava}}, the {{c2::inferior vena cava}}, and the {{c3::coronary sinus}}.
extra: Coronary sinus brings the heart muscle's own blood.

text: The coronary arteries arise from the {{c1::aortic root}}, just above the aortic valve, so the heart is the first territory the aorta supplies.

The three fetal shunts are the {{c1::ductus venosus}} (placenta → IVC, bypassing liver), the {{c2::foramen ovale}} (RA → LA, bypassing lung), and the {{c3::ductus arteriosus}} (pulmonary trunk → aorta).
extra: In the fetus the placenta oxygenates the blood, not the lung.

text: After birth the ductus venosus becomes the {{c1::ligamentum venosum}}, the foramen ovale becomes the {{c2::fossa ovalis}}, and the ductus arteriosus becomes the {{c3::ligamentum arteriosum}}.
extra: First breath drops pulmonary pressure; the shunts close into fibrous scars.

text: The ascending aorta gives only two branches, the {{c1::coronaries}}; then come the arch, thoracic and abdominal aorta, and the bifurcation into the {{c2::common iliac}} arteries.
Organizing principle of the arterial tree: each artery is named by the {{c1::territory it serves}} (renal → kidney, hepatic → liver, splenic → spleen).
extra: A map of territories, not rote names.

text: The aortic arch gives three branches: the {{c1::brachiocephalic trunk}} (splitting into right common carotid + right subclavian), the left common carotid, and the left subclavian.
extra: Right = one trunk that splits; left = vessels arise separately.

text: On the way to the upper limb, the subclavian artery becomes the {{c1::axillary}}, then {{c2::brachial}}, then {{c3::radial and ulnar}} in the forearm.
The brain is supplied by two sources, the {{c1::internal carotids}} (front) and the {{c2::vertebral}} arteries (back), which unite in the {{c3::circle of Willis}}.
extra: The ring is an anastomosis: if one source occludes, blood arrives via the other.

text: Aortic branches split into {{c1::visceral}} (to organs: bronchial, esophageal, pericardial) and {{c2::parietal}} (to the wall: posterior intercostal, superior phrenic).
extra: Same viscera-vs-wall key in thorax and abdomen.

text: The three unpaired visceral branches of the abdominal aorta feed the gut: {{c1::celiac trunk}} (liver, stomach, spleen), {{c2::superior mesenteric}} (small bowel + right colon), and {{c3::inferior mesenteric}} (left colon + rectum).
extra: This territory's returning blood is what detours through the liver.

text: The paired branches of the abdominal aorta, arising laterally to bilateral organs, are the {{c1::suprarenal}}, {{c2::renal}}, and {{c3::gonadal}} arteries.
The aorta bifurcates into common iliacs; each splits into the {{c1::external}} iliac (→ femoral, lower limb) and the {{c2::internal}} iliac (pelvic organs).
Limb veins have three layers: {{c1::deep}} (with the arteries), {{c2::superficial}} (great and small saphenous), and {{c3::perforating}} (pierce the fascia, linking superficial to deep).
extra: Perforator valves drive blood from superficial to deep.

text: When perforating-vein valves fail, blood refluxes and pools in the superficial veins, which swell and become tortuous: {{c1::varicose veins}}.
In the hepatic portal system the mesenteric and splenic veins form the {{c1::portal vein}}, which enters the liver before blood goes on via the hepatic veins to the IVC.
extra: Gut blood is inspected by the liver before general circulation.

text: What makes the portal system special is that blood crosses {{c1::two}} capillary beds in series: the gut, then the liver.
extra: No other territory does this.

text: The {{c1::azygos}} system, ascending along the spine into the SVC, acts as a collateral bridge between the two {{c2::venae cavae}}.
extra: Venous version of the circle-of-Willis idea; rescue route when a cava occludes.

text: Obstruction of the superior vena cava (e.g., mediastinal tumor) causes {{c1::SVC syndrome}}: congested face and neck with dilated collateral chest veins.
extra: The visible dilated veins are the azygos rescue in action.
